who: Isaac was a monk from Beth Qatraye, on the Gulf coast of Arabia. In the late 600s he was made bishop of Nineveh, in today's Iraq. He gave it up after five months and became a hermit in south-west Iran, where he went blind. His writings on prayer, silence and mercy are read across the churches.

roles.name: Monk
roles.line: And a teacher, in Beth Qatraye

roles.name: Hermit
roles.line: In the mountains of south-west Iran

roles.name: Writer

facts.label: Born
facts.text: Some time in the 600s. No year is recorded. At **Beth Qatraye**, on the Gulf coast of Arabia, today **Qatar** and its neighbours.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: In Beth Qatraye. He studied the Church's writings and their commentaries there. Nothing is recorded of his parents.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: **Around 700**, old and blind, at the monastery of Rabban Shabur, near Shushtar in **south-west Iran**. No day or year is recorded.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Isaac of Nineveh**, the name Rome and scholars use. **Isaac Sirin** in Russian. **Abba Isaac** in Greek. His brothers called him **the second Didymus**.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to the Orthodox. The Catholic Church added him to its Roman Martyrology in 2024. In life he was a bishop of the **Church of the East**.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: A woodcut in a Venice book of 1500 shows him as a hooded abbot. It gives him the signs usually given to St Antony: a tau cross, a staff with a bell, and a pig at his feet.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: Short discourses in Syriac, for monks living alone. Three **Parts** are known. Much of the First, of 82 chapters, was put into Greek and read everywhere. In English it is usually called the **Ascetical Homilies**. A Second Part, of 41 chapters, and a Third, of 17, have come to light in modern times.

portrait.alt: A black-and-white woodcut from a 1500 Venice book, labelled Abbate Ysaac, of a hooded, bearded abbot with a halo, leaning on a staff hung with a small bell, with a pig among the flowers at his feet
portrait.credit: Abbate Ysaac, a woodcut in Isaac, De perfectione vitae theoreticae (Venice: Bonetus Locatellus, 1500). BEIC. Public domain.
portrait.caption: *Abbate Ysaac*, a woodcut from the Venice printing of his book, 1500. He is dressed with the signs usually given to St Antony: the tau cross, the bell and the pig. The book was once credited to another Isaac, of Spoleto. BEIC, Milan. Public domain.

east.text: **OCA**, beside Ephrem the Syrian. Also the **Russian Church**, on the old calendar. That is 10 February on today's calendar.
**Greek** churches and **Mount Athos**. St Paisios chose this day.

feasts.note: Why two dates? The Greek calendar had no official day for him. By custom he was named on 28 January, beside Ephrem. St Paisios of Mount Athos had a service written for him and chose 28 September. In the West, the **Catholic Church** added him to its Roman Martyrology in 2024, but the texts that announced it give no day. Many websites say 28 January, but we found no Church text that does. He is not in the **Anglican**, **Episcopal** or **Lutheran** calendars.

traits.title: merciful to every creature
traits.text: He passed on an old monk's teaching as his own. The sum of purity, it says, is “a heart full of mercy unto the whole created nature”. Such a heart prays with tears even for the reptiles, and for those who do it harm.

traits.title: gentle and humble
traits.text: His brothers nicknamed him the second Didymus, “because he was placid and kind and humble, and his speech was meek”. He said he had not lived “one thousandth of what I have written with my hands”.

cite.text: The second early notice; Ascetical Homilies, chapter 22

traits.title: slow to judge
traits.text: He told monks not to scold anyone, “not even those who are very evil in their behaviour”. Weep for the sinner instead, he said, and pray for him, “that thou mayest resemble Christ, Who was not angry with sinners but prayed on their behalf”.

traits.title: generous without asking
traits.text: He told monks to give without sorting people out: “Do not make any distinction between the rich and the poor nor know who is worthy and who is not worthy. Deem all men worthy of bounty on thy part.”

traits.title: hard on himself
traits.text: Three loaves a week, nothing cooked, and reading until he went blind. His own brother, a monk too, begged him by letter to come and visit. Isaac wrote back: “Do not ask from me, o my brother, what gives consolation to body and mind, but let me seek the salvation of my soul.”

traits.title: in love with silence
traits.text: “Silence is a symbol of the future world,” he wrote. “Speech is an organ of this world.” Yet he did not tell monks to shun people: “Be a friend of all men, but a solitary in thy mind.”

traits.title: tired of church quarrels
traits.text: His own church was in communion with no other. Still, he warned monks against “reading books which accentuate the differences between the confessions, with the aim of causing schisms”.

said.lede: Almost all we know of his life comes from two short notices. One is by Isho'dnah of Basra, in the 800s. The other is by an unknown writer, and was printed by the scholar Rahmani. Isaac says very little about himself. After gathering it all, his translator Wensinck wrote: “the real man is in his book.”

quotes.q: He penetrated deeply into the divine mysteries and wrote books on the divine behaviour of solitaries.

cite.text: Book of Chastity, in Wensinck's English

quotes.q: For we confess that we are pupils of Mar Isaac the bishop of Ninive.
quotes.who: Mar Jozadak, writing to his pupil Bushir

cite.text: The second early notice, in Wensinck's English

quotes.q: …had somehow got hold of a copy of the sayings and sermons of “the God-fearing Father Isaac the Syrian,” which he read persistently for years together, understanding very little of it, but perhaps prizing and loving it the more for that.
quotes.who: Dostoevsky, of the old servant Grigory, in The Brothers Karamazov, 1880

quotes.q: Isaac's writings possess passages of singular beauty and elevation, and remind the reader of Thomas à Kempis.
His teaching lays great emphasis on the immensity of divine love and on the need for humanity to respond to this with wonder and humility.
quotes.who: Sebastian Brock, in the Gorgias encyclopedia of the Syriac heritage

moments.title: A monk on the Gulf
moments.text: Isaac was born on the Arabian shore of the Gulf. He studied the Church's writings and their commentaries. Then he became a monk and a teacher in his own country. About 676 George, head of the Church of the East, came to Beth Qatraye. When George went home, he took Isaac with him to Beth Aramaye, in today's Iraq.

cite.text: The second early notice; Brock, e-GEDSH

moments.title: Bishop for five months
moments.text: George made him bishop of Nineveh, in the monastery of Beth Abe. Five months later he gave it up, Isho'dnah says, “for a reason which God knows”. The second notice says that “because of his keen mind and his zeal, he could endure the pastoral function for five months only”. In Isaac's own book, a hermit asks God, “Perhaps, my Lord, grace has been withdrawn from me on account of my episcopal rank?” The answer was no. In the desert, God provided for him. Now men did. His translator took the hermit to be Isaac himself.

cite.text: Isho'dnah; the second notice; Ascetical Homilies, chapter 35

moments.title: Among the hermits
moments.text: He climbed the mountain of Matut in Beth Huzaye, in today's south-west Iran. There he “lived in solitude among the anchorites who were there”. The second notice adds that a man it calls Papa gave him leave to go.

moments.title: Blind, and dictating
moments.text: Later he moved to the monastery of Rabban Shabur. There he came to know the Scriptures deeply. His reading and his hard way of life cost him his sight. After that the brothers wrote down his teaching. He ate three loaves of bread a week, with small vegetables, and never anything cooked. Wensinck adds, without giving a source, that he slept sitting up.

cite.text: Isho'dnah; the second notice; Wensinck, Introduction

moments.title: Three disputed sayings
moments.text: He said three things that the community would not accept. Daniel bar Tubanitha, bishop of Beth Garmai, took offence. What the three were is not known. Isho'dnah adds: “I think that envy was aroused against him by people of the country”. Centuries later, a catalogue of writers says Daniel wrote a “Solution of the difficulties in the writings of Mar Ishak of Nineveh”.

moments.title: The book that crossed every border
moments.text: His church was in communion with no other. Yet in the late 700s or early 800s, two monks of Mar Saba, a Greek monastery near Jerusalem, put much of his First Part into Greek. From there it went into Slavonic, Latin and many more tongues. More than sixty manuscripts survive of a Latin version made around 1200, and an Italian one was printed at Venice in 1500. In 1880 Dostoevsky put his book in the hands of an old servant in The Brothers Karamazov. In 2024 the Catholic Church added Isaac to its Martyrology.

cite.text: Brock, e-GEDSH; Catholic Encyclopedia; Holy See, 2024; L'Osservatore Romano, 2025

words.note: Isaac wrote in Syriac. These lines are from A. J. Wensinck's English of 1923, made from the Syriac. The chapters are numbered as in the Syriac. English versions made from the Greek number them differently.

feature.kicker: Asked what a merciful heart is
feature.q: The burning of the heart unto the whole creation, man, fowls and beasts, demons and whatever exists; so that by the recollection and the sight of them the eyes shed tears on account of the force of mercy which moves the heart by great compassion.
feature.ctx: An old monk's answer, which Isaac makes his own. It is the line he is best known for.

quotes.q: Be on peaceful terms with thy soul; then heaven and earth will be on peaceful terms with thee. Be zealous to enter the treasury within thee; then thou wilt see that which is in heaven. For the former and the latter are one, and entering thou wilt see both. The ladder unto the Kingdom is hidden within thee and within thy soul. Dive into thyself [freed] from sin; there thou wilt find steps along which thou canst ascend.
quotes.who: On the kingdom within. Translations from the Greek word it differently.

quotes.q: As a handful of sand thrown into the ocean, so are the sins of all flesh as compared with God's mind. As a fountain that flows abundantly is not dammed by a handful of earth so the mercy of the Creator is not vanquished by the wickedness of the creatures.
quotes.who: On God's mercy and our sins.

quotes.q: But I say: if the merciful be not even above justice, he is not merciful.
There is no prayer which is heard so soon as when a man asks to be reconciled with those who are angry with him. And when a man charges himself with the fault, this prayer is answered without delay.
This life has been given thee for repentance; do not spend it with various things.
quotes.who: From a chapter of short sayings.

quotes.q: Oft when I was writing these things, my fingers paused on the paper. They could not bear the delight which had fallen into the heart and which made the senses silent.
quotes.who: A rare glimpse of himself as he wrote.

myths.claim: He resigned as bishop over a debt. He asked a lender to give a debtor more time, and the man told him: “Leave your Gospel out of this!”
myths.truth: A later story, from the Arabic tradition, which the OCA still tells. The earliest notice says only that he resigned “for a reason which God knows”. His translator judged the debt story this way: “It has, however, the value of an anecdote only.”

myths.claim: He lived in the 500s, was a monk of Mar Matthew near Nineveh, and went to the desert of Scetis in Egypt.
myths.truth: That is an older account, which the OCA and azbyka.ru still give. Both early notices put him under the Catholicos George, in the later 600s, and scholars follow them. The Catholic Encyclopedia thought the older account was made up by a rival church, “eager to claim so great a writer”.

myths.claim: He is the Syrian hermit Isaac in Gregory the Great's Dialogues, or Isaac of Antioch.
myths.truth: Three different men. Gregory's Isaac came “out of Syria to the city of Spoleto” in Italy, in the 500s. Isaac of Antioch was a priest of the 400s. An Italian version of this Isaac's book was even credited to the Isaac of Spoleto.

cite.text: Gregory, Dialogues, Book 3, chapter 14, with Gardner's note; Catholic Encyclopedia

myths.claim: Only 82 chapters of his survive, and he was a monk from Kurdistan.
myths.truth: Britannica says both, but it is out of date. A Second Part of 41 chapters and a Third of 17 have since come to light. Beth Qatraye, where he was born, is the Gulf coast of Arabia. The monastery in Kurdistan, Beth Abe, is where he was made bishop.

myths.claim: Everything under his name in the Greek Ascetical Homilies is his.
myths.truth: Not quite. The Greek also carries three short works by John of Dalyatha and a shortened letter of Philoxenos under his name. A work called the Book of Grace has been wrongly credited to him too.

myths.claim: He wrote that a merciful heart burns with love for every creature.
myths.truth: The passage is real, but the word love is not in it. The heart burns “unto the whole creation”. It is an old monk's answer, which Isaac makes his own. In the Syriac it is chapter 74. English versions from the Greek number it differently.

stood.lede: Each line is his own, from A. J. Wensinck's English of 1923. His plainest lines on whether hell will end are in the next section.

extras.title: Hard questions
extras.lede: Where Isaac is questioned, in the words of both sides.

items.title: Which church was he in?
items.text: He was a bishop of the **Church of the East**, whose head sat at Seleucia-Ctesiphon. It had not accepted the Council of Ephesus of 431. The Catholic Encyclopedia of 1910 calls him “A Nestorian bishop”. Yet it thinks his three disputed teachings “were of too Catholic a character to be compatible with Nestorian heresy”. He praised Theodore of Mopsuestia, whom a council condemned in 553. His translator found a passage in the Syriac that “looks like a Nestorian addition”, and it is missing from the Greek. In 2024 the Vatican said he belonged to “a Church that was no longer in communion with any other”.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia; Wensinck's note to chapter 33; Holy See, 2024

items.title: A later story
items.text: Some Orthodox hold that he was fully Orthodox. A book about St Paisios of Mount Athos, a monk of the 20th century, reports one testimony. In it, Paisios sees the holy fathers pass before him in a vision. One of them stops and says: “I am Isaac the Syrian. I am completely Orthodox.” The book itself adds: “We are not in a position to endorse or to reject the reliability of this witness.”

cite.text: Hieromonk Isaac, Elder Paisios of Mount Athos (2012), as quoted by OrthoChristian

items.title: Will hell end?
items.text: He wrote that sin had a beginning and will have an end. Hell too had a beginning, “but its end is not known”. Even those in hell, he says, “are tormented with the scourgings of love”. In this First Part he does not say plainly that hell will end. The line our quiz shows for him speaks of grace at the resurrection. These are plainer.
items.quote: Sin, hell and death do not at all exist with God. For they are facts, not persons. Sin is the fruit of will. There was a time, when it was not. And there will be a time, when it will not be. Hell is the fruit of sin; at some time or other it had beginning; but its end is not known.

items.title: Will all be saved?
items.text: His **Second Part** says more openly that hell will end. Those chapters came to light in modern times. Sebastian Brock put them into English in 1995. Metropolitan Hilarion Alfeyev, an Orthodox bishop, wrote a book on Isaac. He calls him one of the greatest theologians of the Orthodox tradition. He does not doubt that Isaac hoped all would be saved. He says this hope is not the same as Origen's teaching, which a council condemned in 553. But he adds a caution:
items.quote: The teaching on universal salvation, which is so explicitly preached by Isaac the Syrian, has never been approved by the Orthodox Church.

cite.text: Hilarion Alfeyev, St Isaac the Syrian, a Theologian of Love and Mercy, a paper given in Rome in 2008, the part on eschatology

items.title: Too hard on monks?
items.text: He asked a great deal. He praised hermits who kept their fast while “feeding upon drugs and dry stubble”. He tells of a recluse who would not go to his dying brother, saying, “should I then honour nature above Christ?” He told a monk who had given everything up that his “rank is higher than that of almsgivers”. But he also held up Macarius the Great, who at ninety walked more than forty miles to bring a sick man fresh bread. And he wrote this:
items.quote: But if he see the brother according to the flesh and to profession, in trouble, or rather: Christ rejected and vexed, and he flee and hide himself, pretending a sham solitude — he that acts thus, is without mercy.

circle.name: George I
circle.text: Head of the Church of the East. He brought Isaac north from the Gulf and made him bishop of Nineveh.

circle.name: Gabriel of Qatar
circle.text: A relative of Isaac's, the second notice says. It calls him the “commentator of the church”.

circle.name: Moses and Sabrisho
circle.text: The bishops of Nineveh before and after him. Sabrisho also left the post, to live as a hermit.

circle.name: Daniel bar Tubanitha
circle.text: Bishop of Beth Garmai. Three things Isaac said scandalised him. He also wrote a book on the difficulties in Isaac's writings.

circle.name: Theodore of Mopsuestia
circle.text: Bishop of Mopsuestia, who died in 428. His writings stood high in Isaac's church. Isaac never met him, but cites him often and calls him “the light of the whole world”.

cite.text: Ascetical Homilies, chapter 19; Wensinck, Introduction; Catholic Encyclopedia

circle.name: Evagrius and Diodore
circle.text: Older writers he quotes by name. Diodore is “the clever and acute Mar Diodorus of Tarsus”. Brock names Evagrius as one of two authors Isaac seems to have valued most.

cite.text: Ascetical Homilies, chapters 1 and 37; Brock, e-GEDSH

circle.name: Abba Arsenius
circle.text: A desert father who would meet no one. Isaac tells how Arsenius sat with visiting fathers and brothers in silence, and sent them away in silence.

circle.name: Macarius and Agathon
circle.text: Desert fathers he held up to monks who looked down on others. Agathon nursed a sick stranger for six months, then said he wished he could give a leper his own body and take the leper's.

circle.name: St Paisios of Mount Athos
circle.text: A 20th-century monk who loved his book. He had a service written for Isaac and chose 28 September as his feast.

death.big: He died old and blind, around 700, at the monastery of Rabban Shabur. No day, illness or last words are recorded.
paras: Both early notices say only that he lived to a great age. Isho'dnah says he “departed this temporary life” and was buried in the monastery. The second notice: “When he had grown old and had reached a high age, he departed unto our Lord.”
The year is not recorded either. Britannica puts it about 700.

saint.big: Yes. The Orthodox honour him as a saint, and the Catholic Church added him to its Roman Martyrology in 2024.

churches.note: His own church. He was one of its bishops
Not in Common Worship or Lesser Feasts and Fasts
Not in the Missouri Synod or ELCA calendars

paras: His own church was cut off from the rest. Even so, the Vatican says, monks of every tradition soon counted him among their saints and fathers.

Pope Francis announced his entry in the Martyrology on 9 November 2024, beside Mar Awa III, head of the Assyrian Church of the East. He called Isaac “one of the most venerated Fathers of the Syro-Oriental tradition, acknowledged as a teacher and a saint by all traditions”. It was done with the agreement of the Assyrian and Chaldean patriarchs.
L'Osservatore Romano explained in 2026 that this is not a canonisation. The Catholic Church is recognising a holiness already proclaimed in other churches.

prayer.intro: He wrote prayers to Christ into his book. This one is from chapter 40.
prayer.q: O Christ, Who art the only strong one, blessed is the man whom Thou supportest and in whose heart are the steps towards Thee. Turn Thou, O Lord, our face away from the world by desire of Thee, so that we see it as it is, without taking shadows for truth. Throw, O Lord, zeal into our heart before death comes, that at the time of our departure we may know for what purpose our entrance in and our departure from this world have served.

tidbits.text: He wrote that wild beasts grow tame when a humble man comes near. They wag their tails and lick his hands and feet. They smell on him, he says, the smell Adam had before the Fall, which Christ gave back to us.
One of his chapters is a run of blunt sayings. Sit with vultures rather than with the greedy, it says, and among lions rather than among the proud. Better a pig's company than a chatterer's.

In 2012 the Assyrian Church of the East opened a monastery named after him in Salida, California. The bishop who opened it, Mar Awa, became that church's patriarch in 2021. In 2024 he was beside Pope Francis when Rome added Isaac to its Martyrology.

cite.text: Assyrian Church News, 2012 and 2021; Holy See Press Office, 2024
